books.section: Topic 3.2 The Seven Years' War (The French and Indian War)

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.
stimulus.text:
| Year | Turning point | What changed |
| 1754 | Seven Years' War begins in North America | Britain and France fight for the continent; the colonies are drawn into an imperial war |
| 1763 | Treaty of Paris ends the war | France loses Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi; Britain takes on a huge war debt |
| 1763 | Proclamation of 1763 | Settlement west of the Appalachians is forbidden; the age of salutary neglect ends |
| 1765–1773 | Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Boston Tea Party | Parliament taxes the colonies for revenue; colonists resist, then organize |
| 1776 | Declaration of Independence | The colonies break with Britain and claim government rests on the consent of the governed |
| 1783 | Treaty of Paris ends the Revolution | Britain recognizes American independence; the new nation holds the land to the Mississippi |
| 1787–1789 | Constitution written and ratified | The weak Articles give way to a stronger federal government |
| 1800 | Election of Thomas Jefferson | Power passes peacefully from one party to another for the first time |

source: original; stimulus is an original data table compiled from the grounding books; stem and options rewritten from fresh-written survivor original-u3-gapfill-period-context-01
stem: Historians mark 1754 as the start of Period 3 with the outbreak of the Seven Years' War in North America. Which of the following best explains why this war marks a turning point between the earlier colonial period and the road to revolution?

options.text: The war ended all British efforts to raise revenue from the colonies, since Parliament decided the colonies had suffered enough.
options.misconception: Britain did the opposite: after 1763 it increased efforts to raise colonial revenue through the Sugar and Stamp Acts.

options.text: The war removed France as a rival in North America, which led Britain to assert tighter control over its colonies.
The war gave the colonies immediate independence, and Britain recognized the United States as a sovereign nation in 1763.
options.misconception: The war ended in 1763 with Britain stronger in North America; independence did not come until 1783.

options.text: The war persuaded Britain to abandon mercantilism and adopt free trade with its colonies.
options.misconception: Britain kept mercantilist policies such as the Navigation Acts; the postwar change was tighter enforcement, not free trade.

rationales.A: Britain did the opposite: after 1763 it increased efforts to raise colonial revenue through the Sugar and Stamp Acts.
rationales.B: Britain's victory in 1763 removed the French threat that had made the colonists depend on British protection. Background: feeling secure and deeply in debt from the war, Britain then imposed new taxes and tighter imperial control, which provoked the colonial resistance that led toward revolution. The war changed the bargain: the colonies no longer needed Britain's shield, and Britain no longer let them govern themselves as before.
rationales.C: The war ended in 1763 with Britain stronger in North America; independence did not come until 1783.
rationales.D: Britain kept mercantilist policies such as the Navigation Acts; the postwar change was tighter enforcement, not free trade.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the table. In 1754 the war begins; by 1763 France is gone from the continent and Britain holds a huge debt.
2. Ask what France's removal meant. The colonists no longer needed British soldiers to protect them from the French.
3. Ask what Britain did next. It tried to make the colonies pay for the war and to rule them more tightly than before.
4. Put it together. A war that began as a fight for empire ended by breaking the old bargain between Britain and its colonies.
Remember: the turning point is not the fighting — it is what victory let Britain do next.
